title: Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894
summary: Turn on one period at a time to watch American Indian land cessions spread across the United States, predict where the next ones will be, and explain why the 1830s cessions are where they are. The map is Charles Royce's record of cessions, so students also ask whose view it shows.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map shows the land the United States gained from American Indian nations by treaty, act of Congress or executive order between 1784 and 1894, as Charles Royce recorded it in the 1890s. There is one layer for each period: before 1830, the 1830s and 1840 to 1894. Only the cessions dated before 1830 are on when the map opens; students turn on the later periods themselves. Each area's pop-up gives the nation named in the record, the date or dates, today's states, the nations that exist today and a link to the treaty or law.

layers.name: Cessions dated 1840 to 1894
layers.shows: Green areas: cessions with a date from 1840 to 1894. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

layers.name: Cessions dated 1830 to 1839
layers.shows: Orange areas: cessions with a date in the 1830s, the decade of the Indian Removal Act. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

layers.name: Cessions dated before 1830
layers.shows: Light blue areas: cessions with a date from 1784 to 1829.
layers.source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

knownIssues.note: Nations today reads "Not listed in the Forest Service data." The source data has no present-day nation for this cession. Question 6 uses it as a source question; the answer notes name nations that exist today.

The boundaries are coarse along rivers: Vicksburg falls just outside the cession Royce shows it in. No question depends on which side of a line a riverside town falls (checked 30 Oct 2026, maps/data/checks/).

compellingQuestion.en: How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?

questions.task: With only Cessions dated before 1830 on, describe where the United States had gained land and which parts of the map are still empty.
frontOfClass: Open The United States bookmark. Only the light blue layer is on.
Open the legend: light blue is cessions dated before 1830.
Ask: where are the light blue areas, east or west of the Mississippi River, north or south?
Ask: which parts of the map are still empty?

steps.en: Open the legend and find the light blue areas: cessions dated before 1830.

ask.en: Where had the United States gained land through cessions before 1830? Which parts of the map are still empty?

answer.where: Cessions dated before 1830 layer, The United States bookmark. Light blue covers most of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas and Florida, much of Alabama, Georgia and Tennessee, southern Michigan, the south and west of Mississippi, and land west of Missouri and Arkansas (today's Kansas and Oklahoma).
answer.accept: Names a region with cessions (the Ohio valley, the lower South, the land just west of the Mississippi) and an empty one: the whole West, the upper Great Lakes (Wisconsin, northern Michigan, Iowa), pockets in the Southeast (northwest Georgia, eastern Alabama, northern and central Mississippi) and the Atlantic coast.
answer.text: The Atlantic coast states are empty because Royce's record starts in 1784: land taken in colonial times, or by the states, isn't on this map. That is a question about the source, which question 6 comes back to.

questions.task: Before turning on the next layer, students predict where the cessions of the 1830s will be and give a reason. They write the prediction down first.
frontOfClass: Keep only Cessions dated before 1830 on.
Ask: where do you expect the cessions of the 1830s to be?
Ask: why there? Have students write the prediction down before anyone turns on the next layer.

steps.en: Keep only Cessions dated before 1830 on.
Look at the empty parts of the map, east and west of the Mississippi River.
Write your prediction before you turn on any other layer.

ask.en: Where do you expect the cessions of the 1830s to be? Why there?

fill.en: I predict the 1830s cessions will be in ______________ because ______________.

answer.accept: Any prediction with a reason drawn from question 1: for example, the empty pockets in the Southeast surrounded by earlier cessions, the land next to the Great Lakes, or the West. Predictions are checked in question 3, not marked right or wrong here.

questions.task: Turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 and compare the orange areas with the prediction. Use The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839.
Ask: where are the orange areas? Was your prediction right?
Open The Southeast bookmark, then The Old Northwest.
Ask: what do the orange areas in the Southeast have in common with the empty pockets you found in question 1?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839.
Open The Southeast bookmark, then The Old Northwest bookmark.
Compare the orange areas with your prediction.

ask.en: Where were the cessions of the 1830s? Was your prediction right? What do the orange areas in the Southeast have in common with the empty pockets you found before 1830?

answer.where: Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 layer, with The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks. Orange fills most of the empty pockets in the Southeast: northern and central Mississippi, eastern and northwestern Alabama, northwest Georgia and corners of Tennessee and North Carolina. In the north it covers most of Wisconsin, much of Iowa, northern Michigan and northern Indiana. There are also orange areas inside today's Kansas and Oklahoma.
answer.accept: Says the 1830s cessions are mostly east of the Mississippi, in the Southeast and around the Great Lakes, and that in the Southeast they fill the gaps left between earlier cessions; compares this honestly with the prediction.
answer.text: The orange areas in Kansas and Oklahoma are cessions of land there, some by nations that had been moved west; students can open one, but no question depends on it.

questions.task: Open orange cessions in the Southeast and read the nation, the date and the kind of document; use the Indian Removal Act (1830), in Before you start, to explain the pattern.
frontOfClass: Make sure Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 is on, and open The Southeast bookmark.
Click the large orange area in central Mississippi and read the pop-up: the nation, the date and the link.
Click two more orange areas: eastern Alabama and northwest Georgia.
Ask: which nations, which years, and what kind of document?
Ask: the Indian Removal Act was signed in May 1830. How might it explain why these cessions came in the 1830s, and why here?

steps.en: Make sure Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 is on, and open The Southeast bookmark.
Click three orange areas: central Mississippi, eastern Alabama and northwest Georgia.
For each, write down the nation, the date and the kind of document the link names.

ask.en: Which nations, which years and what kind of document? Using the Indian Removal Act in Before you start, why might these cessions have come in the 1830s, and why here?

answer.where: Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 layer, The Southeast bookmark, pop-ups. Central Mississippi: Choctaw, September 27, 1830 (Today's states: AL; MS). Eastern Alabama: Creek, March 24, 1832. Northwest Georgia: Cherokee, December 29, 1835 (AL; GA; NC; TN). Others students may open: Chickasaw, October 20, 1832 (northern Mississippi, AL; MS; TN); Seminole, May 9, 1832, in central Florida (that area also has the date September 18, 1823). Each link reads Treaty text.
answer.accept: Connects the dates to the Indian Removal Act: after May 1830 the President could negotiate removal treaties with nations east of the Mississippi, and within about five years the Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Cherokee had ceded the last of their land in the Southeast. Explains why here: these were the nations' remaining homelands, surrounded by land already ceded and by settlers who wanted it. Strong answers say the treaties were made under pressure and note that the map alone can't show why; the Act is the evidence.
answer.text: The Treaty of New Echota (December 1835) was signed by the minority Treaty Party; Principal Chief John Ross, the Cherokee government and most Cherokees opposed it, and 3,352 Cherokees signed an 1836 petition asking the Senate not to ratify it (National Archives, DocsTeach). The National Archives says Jackson's administration negotiated almost 70 removal treaties, and nearly 50,000 people were moved to Indian Territory.

questions.task: Turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 and describe how the pattern changed, using The Plains and the West bookmark.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894.
Open The United States bookmark, then The Plains and the West.
Ask: where are the green areas, and how is that different from the 1830s?
Ask: which parts of the country have no cessions at all, and why might that be?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894.
Open The United States bookmark, then The Plains and the West bookmark.

ask.en: How did the pattern change after 1840? Which parts of the country have no cessions at all on this map?

answer.where: Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 layer. Green covers almost all of the West: the Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the Southwest, California and the Pacific Northwest, and Minnesota. It also covers most of today's Oklahoma, where nations moved from the East later ceded land again. Still empty: New England, the Mid-Atlantic states, Virginia, West Virginia and most of Kentucky.
answer.accept: Says the cessions moved west of the Mississippi and across the whole West after 1840, and that by 1894 almost all the land west of the Mississippi had been ceded; notes the empty East and links it to the record starting in 1784.

questions.task: Read the note at the end of a pop-up and the Nations today line for two cessions, including the Creek cession of 1832, and ask whose view of these transactions the map shows.
frontOfClass: Click the Cherokee cession in northwest Georgia and read the note in italics at the end of the pop-up.
Ask: who recorded these cessions, when, and from whose records?
Click the Creek cession in eastern Alabama and read Nations today.
Ask: what is missing here, and what might the nations named in the pop-ups say about the same transactions?

steps.en: Click the Cherokee cession in northwest Georgia and read the note in italics at the end of the pop-up.
Click the Creek cession in eastern Alabama and read Nations today.

ask.en: Who recorded these cessions, and from whose records? What is missing from the Creek pop-up? What might the nations named in the pop-ups say about the same transactions?

answer.where: Pop-up note: Royce mapped this in the 1890s from United States records, so it shows how the federal government recorded the transaction, and the boundary is approximate. The Creek cession of March 24, 1832 reads "Not listed in the Forest Service data" under Nations today.
answer.accept: Says the map is a federal record made decades later, so it shows transactions as the United States recorded them; notes the missing present-day nation for the Creek cession (the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma is one nation that exists today); suggests that the nations might describe some cessions as forced, disputed or signed by people who did not speak for them, and that their own records would tell a different story.
answer.text: Royce's schedule (linked in each pop-up) is a federal document from 1899. The layer was digitized by the USDA Forest Service, which says the data are for information only, not for deciding title or boundaries.

final.teacher: Students answer the compelling question with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. Accept answers that describe the pattern over time (east and south before 1830, the Southeast and Great Lakes in the 1830s, the West after 1840), connect the 1830s to the Indian Removal Act with dates from the pop-ups, and say that the map is a federal record. The students' own questions are a good place to start the next lesson, for example on the Trail of Tears.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map raises for you.

objectives: Describe where the United States had gained American Indian land before 1830, using the Cessions dated before 1830 layer and the legend.
Make a prediction about the next period from the map, then turn on the 1830s layer and test it.
Read the nation, date and kind of document in the pop-ups of three 1830s cessions in the Southeast.
Explain the 1830s pattern in the Southeast using the Indian Removal Act (1830) as evidence.
Evaluate the map as a source: who recorded the cessions, when, and whose view is missing.
discussion: Your prediction in question 2: what did you base it on, and what did the 1830s layer show that you didn't expect?
The map shows where and when, but not why. What other evidence would you need to explain a single cession, such as the Cherokee cession of 1835?
Royce called these areas cessions. Is cession a fair word for all of them? What other words might the nations named in the pop-ups use?

differentiation.support: Do questions 1 and 3 from the front with the legend open, and give pairs the three places to click in question 4 (central Mississippi, eastern Alabama, northwest Georgia) marked on a printed screenshot.
differentiation.stretch: Open the Treaty text link for the Cherokee cession of 1835 and find one article about moving west; compare it with what the pop-up and Before you start say.

resources.title: Jackson's Message to Congress on Indian Removal (1830)
On Exhibit: the Indian Removal Act
Analyzing the Petition Against the Treaty of New Echota
Indian Land Cessions in the United States (Royce, 1899), maps and schedule

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use all three layers in order (where light blue, orange and green fall), pop-up names and dates for at least two 1830s Southeast cessions (Choctaw, September 27, 1830; Creek, March 24, 1832; Cherokee, December 29, 1835), the Indian Removal Act of May 1830, and the pop-up note on who recorded the map.
assessment.exemplar: The United States gained American Indian land mostly by treaty, and the cessions moved across the map in a clear order. With only the light blue layer on, the cessions before 1830 cover Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri and most of the lower South, but there are empty pockets in Mississippi, eastern Alabama and northwest Georgia. When I turned on the orange 1830s layer, those pockets filled in. The pop-ups show the Choctaw cession on September 27, 1830, the Creek on March 24, 1832 and the Cherokee on December 29, 1835, and each link says Treaty text. The Indian Removal Act of May 1830 let the President make removal treaties with nations east of the Mississippi, so within five years the last homelands in the Southeast were ceded. After 1840 the green layer covers almost the whole West. The pop-up note says Royce made the map in the 1890s from United States records, and the Creek pop-up doesn't list a nation today, so this is the federal government's record. The nations might call these cessions forced rather than agreed.

beforeYouStart.en: A cession is land one side gives up to another, usually by treaty. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act, which let the President make treaties to move American Indian nations living east of the Mississippi River to land in the West. This map comes from Charles Royce, who worked for the federal government and recorded every cession in the 1890s.

readingTheMap.en: There is one layer for each period: light blue for cessions dated before 1830, orange for the 1830s and green for 1840 to 1894; use the legend. Only the light blue layer is on when the map opens: turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. An area with dates in two periods shows in both layers, and its pop-up lists every date. The map shows where and when, not how many acres. Boundaries are approximate.

reflection.en: Turning the layers on one at a time, what did you notice about how the cessions spread that you might have missed on a finished map?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The map opens with only Cessions dated before 1830 on. Students turn on the 1830s layer in question 3 and the 1840 to 1894 layer in question 5, so ask them not to turn layers on early: question 2's prediction only works before the reveal. The map has no place names on the cessions; the basemap shows today's states and cities.

misconceptions.claim: Empty parts of the map, such as New England and Virginia, were never American Indian land.
misconceptions.response: Royce's record starts in 1784. Land taken in colonial times, or by the states, isn't on this map.

misconceptions.claim: A cession means a nation chose to sell its land.
misconceptions.response: Many cessions were made under pressure or disputed; the map is the federal government's record of them, as the pop-up note says.

misconceptions.claim: Bigger colored areas mean more land was taken in that period.
misconceptions.response: The map shows where and when, not acres, and an area with dates in two periods appears in both layers.

standards.text: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.

Analyze the reasons for the removal and resettlement of Cherokee Indians during the Jacksonian era, including the Indian Removal Act, Worcester v. Georgia, and the Trail of Tears (partial: this lesson covers the reasons and the Indian Removal Act; the Trail of Tears is the next map).
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Discuss the impact of westward expansion on cultural practices and migration patterns of Native Americans, African slave populations and other minority groups (partial: Native Americans).
